analysis.one_liner: Protects health care workers from retaliation when they raise patient safety concerns.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 with no cosponsors and was sent to three House committees; it has not had a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, and other health care facilities to punish a doctor, nurse, or other practitioner for speaking up about patient safety, including concerns about staffing levels, equipment, or quality of care. A practitioner who is fired or demoted within 180 days of raising a concern would have a legal presumption that it was retaliation, and could win actual damages, attorney's fees, and punitive damages of up to $1 million, with class actions allowed across facilities under the same ownership. It would also void gag clauses and release whistleblowing practitioners from non-compete agreements tied to the facility, and require Medicare-participating providers to set up an anonymous safety-reporting system.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care practitioners, including nurses, doctors, therapists, and technicians at every kind of licensed facility, would gain a private right to sue for retaliation with a presumption in their favor, class-action leverage, freedom from gag clauses and certain non-competes, and protection from having their safety complaints used against them in later malpractice actions. Patients would benefit indirectly, because safety concerns about understaffing, supplies, and quality of care could reach regulators, the Joint Commission, and — after a 90-day waiting period — the press without the messenger facing termination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care workers and their patients

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits facilities from retaliating against practitioners for communicating patient safety concerns to supervisors, state regulators, government officials, patient safety organizations, or — after 90 days without corrective action — the news media.
Creates a rebuttable presumption that any adverse employment action within 180 days of a safety complaint is retaliation, shifting the burden of proof to the facility.

Lets practitioners recover actual damages, attorney's fees, and punitive damages of up to $1 million, and authorizes class actions where facilities under common ownership share a pattern of retaliation, with class awards that can reach $500,000 or 1% of the defendant's net worth.
Voids any contract clause that would prohibit a provider from speaking truthfully about quality of care, and releases a whistleblower from non-compete agreements tied to the facility in question.
Requires Medicare-participating providers to establish an anonymous patient safety reporting mechanism and a process for investigating the concerns that come in.
Bars the practitioner's patient safety communications from being used to draw an adverse inference about quality of care in later professional liability actions.

analysis.who_pays: Health care facilities, which would face damage awards including punitive damages and class-action penalties, and — because retaliation by staffing companies or management services companies is attributed back to the facility — the hospitals and nursing homes that rely on contract staffing. Facilities would also bear the cost of building anonymous reporting systems if they participate in Medicare, and would lose the contractual tools (gag clauses, certain non-competes) used to keep practitioners quiet.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and staffing companies

drawbacks.text: A practitioner must first file with the state licensing authority (and, for hospitals, the Joint Commission) and wait until the investigation finishes or 180 days pass before suing, which can delay any recovery.
Going to the press is allowed only 90 days after reporting internally, so genuinely urgent public warnings could legally wait.

The definition of a protected 'patient safety concern' is broad — it covers staffing practices and equipment sufficiency — and the 180-day presumption means any firing or demotion of a recent complainant can be treated as retaliation; facilities argue this would invite costly litigation over ordinary personnel decisions. The bill does allow suits against practitioners who raise concerns in bad faith.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is straightforward and hard to argue against: workers who report conditions that could hurt patients should not lose their jobs for it, and the burden-shifting presumption plus damages make the right real rather than symbolic. The honest cost is litigation exposure for facilities — a broad definition of protected speech, a generous presumption of retaliation, and large class-action awards would push some disputes into court that a narrower statute would keep out. The pre-filing requirements with state regulators and the Joint Commission help filter meritless claims but also slow down legitimate ones. On balance the protections are the bill's substance; the compliance and litigation costs fall on facilities whose interest in quieting staffing complaints is precisely what the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced April 15, 2026 and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — where it has sat without any hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon (D-PA) introduced the Patient Safety and Whistleblower Protections Act on April 15, 2026.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and additionally to the Ways and Means and Judiciary Committees, for the provisions falling under each one's jurisdiction.
No members of either party had signed on as cosponsors as of the latest record.
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history after the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to act. Health care facilities, staffing companies, and management services companies face no new anti-retaliation liability, no punitive damages exposure, and no requirement to build anonymous safety-reporting systems, because the bill has not advanced. The practitioner who brought it has gained a floor conversation at most.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospital and facility operators, so far

for.name: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would bar health care facilities from retaliating against practitioners who raise patient safety concerns.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of opposition is not yet in the record.

industries.note: The bill imposes private lawsuits with punitive damages up to $1 million and class-action penalties on facilities that retaliate against practitioners who report safety problems, including understaffing. Facilities' financial interest in keeping staffing complaints quiet runs against patients' and workers' interest in getting those complaints heard.

industries.industry: Health care staffing and management services companies
industries.note: Retaliation by a staffing company or management services company is attributed to the facility that was the subject of the complaint, making the facility liable and letting it seek contribution from the contractor. Their cost is a direct reduction in their ability to act on staffing disputes without facility-level legal exposure.

Providers participating in Medicare would have to set up an anonymous patient safety reporting channel and a process to investigate reports, a modest compliance cost attached to a federal benefit. The requirement applies to the same providers the reporting system is meant to help hold accountable.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and referrals to three committees about two months into its life, the bill is at the stage where most House bills stop: committee referral with no scheduled hearing. It would need its sponsor to recruit cosponsors and committee chairs to schedule markups in multiple jurisdictions — a heavy lift — to reach a floor vote before this Congress ends in January 2027.
